extracted.intended_audience: general readers of essays and philosophy; students of human judgment and moral skepticism
extracted.subtask_description: An early modern essay (Montaigne) reflecting on human judgment, the variability of belief, customs, passions, and practical wisdom; mixes anecdote, classical citation, and philosophical skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions dislocate reason
rubrics_metrics.description: “the dislocation that passions cause in our reason” — passions, fury, or the extirpation of reason (madness, the image of death) change perception and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that strong passions alter the soul's sight and judgment (images appear different, advantages seem larger, difficulties appear easier) and produce volatile convictions; examples include sudden love or desire that later evaporates like lightning. The text warns not to treat decisions or truths formed in such heated states as reliably founded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize observed effects over speculative novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: “I replied that I had rather follow effects than reason.” — prefer practical, observed outcomes to speculative arguments or novel theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne prefers experience and effects as grounds for trust: he resists Paracelsus’s new medical system and a self-proclaimed demonstrator about winds, arguing that visible, practical consequences (what actually works) are more trustworthy than ingenious but untested demonstrations. Use real-world outcomes to evaluate bold claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of new doctrines (beliefs change over time)
rubrics_metrics.description: “So that when any new doctrine presents itself to us, we have great reason to mistrust, and to consider that, before that was set on foot, the contrary had been generally received.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites changes from Ptolemaic to Copernican astronomy and historical reversals to show that prevailing beliefs are often overturned. When confronted with new doctrines, one should recall historical shifts and withhold full credence until corroborated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and temporal variability undermines universality claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “there is nothing so extreme that is not allowed by the custom of some nation or other.” — laws, customs, and morals vary widely between peoples and ages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay lists many divergent customs (marriage practices, funerary rites, dietary rules, religious ceremonies, legal norms) to show that practices deemed monstrous in one society are honorable in another. Any claim of universal moral truth should account for this variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of natural/perpetual laws are doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: “they say, that there are some firm, perpetual, and immovable, which they call natural… a sign that it is a mark as doubtful as the rest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne questions the idea that a small list of 'natural laws' can be demonstrated by universality, noting that supposed natural laws are contested and contradicted by many peoples. Universality of approval is the only plausible sign of a natural law, and even that sign often fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish civic/legal duty from universal truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “what our reason advises us to, as the most likely, is generally for every one to obey the laws of his country… but Truth ought to have a like and universal visage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the laws of one's country may be practical advice but does not establish universal moral truth; obligations grounded in local law are accidental and should not be conflated with eternal equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer to wiser counsel when personally weak
rubrics_metrics.description: “He that finds himself weak ought to answer… he will speak with his counsel, or refer himself to the wiser, from whom he received his instruction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one recognizes personal intellectual weakness or inability to answer, the prudent course is to consult wiser persons rather than adopt unfounded beliefs. Montaigne presents this as practical humility rather than ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desires and imagined goods can be harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: “what is pleasing to us is not always good for us.” (King Midas anecdote; Montaigne’s own wish for the Order of St. Michael became devalued)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns that attaining what one fervently desires may produce misery or unintended consequences. Evaluate wished-for outcomes critically; desire is an unreliable indicator of what is truly beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason is malleable and can justify opposing views
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus reason finds appearances for divers effects; ‘tis a pot with two ears that a man may take by the right or left.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Aristippus vs Diogenes, Lycurgus’s re-interpretation of theft) show that reason can be employed to support contradictory practices; therefore, one should beware of purely rhetorical or plausible-sounding arguments and seek firmer grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal judgments and institutional decisions are inconsistent and biased
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge wrote in the margin 'a question for a friend' because truth was so controverted; advocates and judges accommodate causes to their will; courts decide contrary to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes the instability and partiality of legal practice—rulings shift between courts and judges. This implies skepticism toward treating judicial or institutional verdicts as definitive moral truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate, place, and circumstance shape human faculties and morals
rubrics_metrics.description: “Et plaga codi non solum ad robor corporum, sed etiam animorum facit… The air of Athens is subtle and thin… wherefore the Thebans are looked upon as more heavy-witted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical environment (climate, soil, air) influences not only bodies but temperaments, dispositions, and capacities for particular arts or virtues. Evaluations of peoples or practices must account for environmental and situational causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of religious motifs across cultures is meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'vain shadows of our religion' observed among distant peoples (beliefs resembling purgatory, rituals, mitres, celibacy, crosses) are 'testimonies of its dignity and divinity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne treats cross-cultural similarities in religious practice as evidence that certain religious truths or structures may transcend local invention—this is offered as a reason not to dismiss familiar religion as purely provincial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate testimonial likelihood beyond rhetorical plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “The facility that good wits have of rendering every thing likely they would recommend… this evidently shows the weakness of their testimony.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clever or eloquent presentation does not make a claim true. Montaigne urges scrutiny of testimony and argument quality beyond how plausibly or attractively it is put.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compile and classify opinions with life-examples for clearer assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne’s wish that a learned man should 'collect into a register… the opinions of the ancient philosophers… with the application of the lives of the authors and their disciples to their own precepts, in memorable accidents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He recommends a systematic, exemplified compilation of philosophical doctrines connected to biographical and anecdotal evidence to better judge doctrines’ practical value—an implicit standard for evaluating philosophical claims.
